title: First Diwali After Gulf War Finds India Spending Less, Using Savings
excerpt: LocalCircles puts average urban festive spending at Rs 20,000 and the total at Rs 1.97 lakh crore, 6% below 2025, as 5.54% inflation, $101 oil and record gold prices tighten household budgets.
body:
• Urban Indian households expect to spend about Rs 20,000 on average this festive season, with total urban festive spending estimated at Rs 1.97 lakh crore — 6% below last year's Rs 2.10 lakh crore, LocalCircles' survey of over 67,000 responses found.
  • Inflation is doing the squeezing: retail inflation hit 5.54% in September, food inflation 7.74%, Brent crude traded near $101 a barrel — over 50% higher than a year ago — after the Gulf war disrupted energy supplies.
  • 83% of households planning festive purchases expect to dip into savings, and 34% will fund 25% or more from savings; 31% plan no discretionary spending at all.
  • For NRI families gifting or remitting for Diwali: gold near Rs 1.50 lakh per 10 grams and silver near Rs 2.26 lakh per kg mean jewellery is only 6% of planned purchases — cash gifts and clothing (72%) are carrying this Diwali.

India heads into its first Diwali since the Gulf war with households planning to spend less and fund what they do spend from savings. LocalCircles' Mood of the Consumer survey, covering more than 67,000 responses across 307 districts, estimates average urban festive spending at about Rs 20,000 per household and total urban spending at Rs 1.97 lakh crore, down 6% from Rs 2.10 lakh crore in 2025, according to the full LocalCircles report. Last year's figure had been lifted by GST rate cuts that took effect on September 22, 2025; there is no comparable tax tailwind this year.

The price data behind the caution

The squeeze is measurable, not just sentiment. Retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, its eleventh consecutive monthly increase, while food inflation jumped to 7.74% from 5.97% and onion prices more than doubled year-on-year. A home-cooked vegetarian thali cost about 10% more than a year earlier. Wholesale inflation reached 11.39% in September, signalling more pressure still in the pipeline.

The energy link runs through the Gulf war. Brent crude traded at about $101 a barrel on October 6, over 50% higher than a year ago, as disrupted Gulf supplies kept oil elevated. That feeds transport, edible oil and manufacturing costs across the basket. Sweets show it plainly: sugar prices rose 29.8% year-on-year in September, sugar and confectionery inflation hit 13.8%, and prepared sweets rose 9.4%, according to official price data reported by Indulge Express. Raisins and munakka rose 10.4% and cashews 4%, pushing up kaju katli and dry-fruit gift boxes.

On October 7 the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, its first hike in over three and a half years, and Governor Sanjay Malhotra said rate cuts are off the table near term. The RBI expects inflation to peak at 6.0% in the October-December quarter — the festive quarter itself. If passed on in full, the hike adds about Rs 817 a month to the EMI on a Rs 50 lakh, 25-year home loan.

Where the money still goes

Spending has narrowed, not vanished. Of households planning purchases, 72% will buy clothing and fashion, 45% home appliances and furniture, 45% travel and holidays, and 39% gourmet food and gifting. Only 6% plan jewellery, with gold at about Rs 1.50 lakh per 10 grams and silver at about Rs 2.26 lakh per kg on MCX on October 7. Nine percent expect to spend over Rs 1 lakh; 30% expect Rs 10,000 to Rs 1 lakh; 18% will stay under Rs 10,000.

Early sales match the split, Outlook Business reported: Meesho's first-day orders rose 75% year-on-year in fashion, beauty and festive decor, while Counterpoint Research expects festive smartphone volumes to fall 12% as chip costs lift prices, even as value rises 5%. Redseer data cited there put items under Rs 500 at about half of festive orders, with average order values 7-8% lower than last year.

What to watch after Diwali

The funding pattern is the risk. With 83% of spending households dipping into savings and 16% relying on savings entirely, this Diwali is partly paid for from past income rather than current earnings. If inflation peaks as the RBI expects and then eases, that cushion can rebuild. If oil stays above $100 into the wedding season, households that drew down savings now enter 2027 with a thinner buffer — and retailers face a post-Diwali test of whether festive demand was borrowed from the months ahead.
